summary: Astronomers observe the same sky across the electromagnetic spectrum — radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray — because each band reveals different objects and processes. The central ideas for ages 11-13: (1) different wavelengths carry different information about the same object, so observing in many bands is like using several senses at once, and many telescopes detect light our eyes cannot see rather than merely magnifying; (2) Earth's atmosphere blocks UV, X-ray, gamma-ray, much of the infrared and parts of the microwave range, while letting visible light, radio and some microwave and near-infrared through 'windows' (the CMB was first detected by a ground-based antenna, though space missions map it best), which is why many telescopes must fly in space — to escape absorption, not to get closer to the stars. Ground each band with one vivid phenomenon (microwave/CMB, IR/dust-piercing to early galaxies and forming stars, UV/hot young stars, visible/planets and familiar structure, X-ray & gamma/black holes, pulsars, violent explosions) and contrast Hubble (mainly visible/UV/near-IR) with JWST (infrared) to make the 'different eyes' idea tangible.
misconceptions: 'Telescopes just magnify to see faint things' — many telescopes detect wavelengths our eyes can't see at all; it's about capturing invisible light, not only making things bigger
'Visible light is the normal/real light and the rest is exotic' — visible is just the band our eyes evolved for; every band is equally 'real' light
'We put telescopes in space to get closer to the stars' — the distance saved is negligible; it's to escape the atmosphere that blocks certain wavelengths and blurs images
'Infrared is just heat, not light' — infrared IS light (EM radiation) with a longer wavelength than visible; warm objects emit it
'All telescopes work the same way' — X-ray telescopes need grazing-incidence mirrors and there are no focusing gamma-ray telescopes; different bands need fundamentally different instruments
'Hubble and JWST see the same thing' — Hubble is mainly visible/UV while JWST is infrared, so JWST sees cooler, dustier, more distant (redshifted) objects Hubble cannot

activities.title: Transform one object across the spectrum
steps: Study genuine multiwavelength images of a single rich target (e.g. a star-forming nebula or the galactic centre) ordered radio→microwave→infrared→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma.

For each band, if an interactive is available, drag a wavelength slider that cross-fades the central image to that band's real view; otherwise step through the ordered strip of real images side by side.
Observe and name what appears or disappears: dust lanes that hide stars in visible light melt away in infrared to reveal newborn stars; a knot of superheated gas blazes into view in X-ray.
Write one sentence per band stating the specific phenomenon that band uniquely reveals about THIS object.
Explain in your own words why the images differ: each wavelength reveals different physical processes at different temperatures and energies, not the same scene merely recoloured.
activities.insight: The same patch of sky looks utterly different in each band because different wavelengths reveal different phenomena — so combining bands builds a fuller picture than any single one, and much of this is about detecting light our eyes cannot see, not just magnifying it.

activities.title: Why does it have to fly? The atmosphere decides
steps: Read or examine an atmospheric-opacity ('windows') chart showing which wavelengths penetrate to the ground and which are absorbed.

For each band, decide and record: does this light reach the ground, or is it blocked? (Radio and visible pass through, along with some microwave and near-infrared windows; UV, X-ray, gamma, much of the infrared and parts of the microwave range are blocked.)

Sort real telescopes into 'works from the ground' (e.g. radio dish) versus 'must be in space' (e.g. an X-ray observatory, or a mid/far-infrared observatory such as JWST), justifying each placement by whether its band reaches the ground.

Answer: distinguish the atmosphere BLURRING visible light (which a higher-altitude ground telescope, or adaptive optics, can partly reduce) from the atmosphere BLOCKING whole bands entirely (which no ground telescope of any size can overcome).
State in one sentence why an X-ray telescope must be launched into space — because the atmosphere absorbs X-rays completely, so they never reach the ground, not because space is closer to the stars.
activities.insight: Earth's atmosphere absorbs certain wavelengths entirely, so telescopes for those bands must operate in space; the reason is escaping absorption, not reducing distance or only sharpening the view.

activities.title: Hubble vs JWST: two eyes, two universes
steps: Compare the wavelength coverage of Hubble (mainly visible and ultraviolet, with some near-infrared) and JWST (infrared).
Look at the same astronomical target as each telescope would capture it, noting what JWST reveals that Hubble cannot.
Explain why an infrared telescope can see earlier, dustier, more distant (redshifted) galaxies than a mainly visible telescope.

Write a short justification, as if advising an observing team, for choosing JWST over Hubble for imaging the first galaxies — referencing dust penetration and redshift of very distant light into the infrared.
Optionally, discuss with a peer or in a role-play 'interview a JWST scientist' why the telescope had to be flown far from Earth and kept very cold to do infrared work.
activities.insight: Hubble and JWST do not see the same thing: because they observe different bands, JWST can detect cooler, dustier and more distant objects, many of which are faint or invisible to a mainly visible telescope.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, sort, and sequence the spectrum
steps: Match each band to the phenomenon it uniquely reveals (e.g. microwave↔cosmic microwave background, X-ray↔matter around black holes, infrared↔newborn stars behind dust, radio↔cold gas clouds).
Sort telescopes into 'works from the ground' versus 'must be in space' and give the reason (which band reaches the ground).

Sequence the bands in order of wavelength (radio→microwave→infrared→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma) and describe the matching trend: shorter wavelength always means more energy per photon, and for glowing objects shorter wavelengths usually point to hotter, more violent sources while longer ones usually point to cooler ones.

Note the instrument idea: different bands need fundamentally different instruments — for example X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors, and gamma-ray telescopes usually can't focus gamma rays with mirrors at all, so they use particle-detector methods instead.
activities.insight: The spectrum is an ordered scale linking wavelength, energy and temperature, and each band maps to distinct phenomena and often distinct instrument designs.

checkQuestion: A visible-light telescope works fine on a mountaintop here on Earth, but an X-ray telescope MUST be launched into space to work at all — and it's not just about getting a sharper view. Why can't an X-ray telescope work from the ground? And why do astronomers bother observing in X-rays, infrared and radio at all, instead of just visible light? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: An X-ray telescope must be in space because Earth's atmosphere completely BLOCKS (absorbs) X-rays, gamma rays and much infrared — they never reach the ground at all, so no ground telescope could detect them however big or high it is. Visible light and radio waves pass through 'windows' in the atmosphere, so those telescopes work from the ground. Astronomers observe across the whole electromagnetic spectrum because different wavelengths reveal different things: radio shows cold gas clouds and pulsars, infrared sees through dust to newborn stars and distant galaxies, visible shows stars like the Sun, X-rays reveal super-hot gas and matter swirling around black holes, and gamma rays flag the most violent explosions. Each band is real light carrying information the others miss.
